chunks.title: Namespace and label conventions for production
chunks.content:
Namespace and label conventions for production

Create a dedicated Namespace for each environment or team with labels: environment, managed-by, team. Standard labels applied to all resources: app (service name), version (semver), environment. Namespaces provide resource isolation, RBAC scope, and NetworkPolicy boundaries.

Decision rules:
- Use one namespace per environment (production, staging, development) — do not mix environments
- Apply consistent labels (app, version, environment) to all resources to enable selectors and monitoring
- Set managed-by: terraform or managed-by: helm on namespaces created via IaC

Trade-offs:
- Fine-grained namespace-per-team increases isolation but requires more RBAC and NetworkPolicy configuration

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying production workloads to the default namespace
- Omitting labels — makes resource selection, monitoring dashboards, and GitOps tooling fragile

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- EKS namespaces map to IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) scope for granular AWS API access control

chunks.title: Production-ready Deployment manifest
chunks.content:
Production-ready Deployment manifest

Production Deployment: 3 replicas, RollingUpdate strategy (maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 for zero-downtime), dedicated ServiceAccount (automountServiceAccountToken: false), podAntiAffinity across nodes, pod-level SecurityContext (runAsNonRoot, seccompProfile RuntimeDefault), container-level SecurityContext (allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities drop ALL), resource requests/limits, env from ConfigMap/Secret, liveness + readiness + startup probes, emptyDir volumes for writable paths, terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60.

Decision rules:
- Set maxUnavailable: 0 for zero-downtime rolling deployments — pods are added before old ones are removed
- Use pinned image tags (myapp:1.0.0) — never :latest in production
- Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds >= timeout of your longest in-flight request to allow graceful shutdown

Trade-offs:
- maxUnavailable: 0 requires cluster capacity for maxSurge extra pods during rollout
- podAntiAffinity with preferredDuringScheduling may not spread pods if cluster nodes are insufficient

Anti-patterns:
- Using :latest image tag — non-deterministic and bypasses rollback capability
- Not setting terminationGracePeriodSeconds — pods may be killed mid-request
- Missing startup probe for slow-starting apps — liveness probe will kill the pod before it finishes initializing

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use Karpenter on EKS for just-in-time node provisioning to support rolling surge capacity

chunks.title: Service (ClusterIP) and Ingress with TLS
chunks.content:
Service (ClusterIP) and Ingress with TLS

Service type ClusterIP on port 80 -> targetPort 8000. Never NodePort or LoadBalancer directly for internal services. Ingress with nginx ingress class, cert-manager annotation (letsencrypt-prod), ssl-redirect: true, proxy-body-size: 10m, rate-limit: 100. TLS spec with hosts array and secretName for certificate.

Decision rules:
- Use ClusterIP as the default Service type — expose externally only via Ingress
- Set nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rate-limit on all public-facing Ingress resources
- Use cert-manager with Let's Encrypt for automated TLS certificate management

Trade-offs:
- Nginx Ingress with rate-limit annotation is per-server, not distributed — use Redis-backed rate limiting for distributed enforcement

Anti-patterns:
- Using NodePort or direct LoadBalancer Service types without an Ingress — bypasses centralized TLS and rate limiting
- Not setting proxy-body-size — allows unbounded request body sizes

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- On EKS, use AWS Load Balancer Controller with Ingress class alb for native ALB integration and ACM certificate management

chunks.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) for automatic scaling
chunks.content:
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) for automatic scaling

HPA (autoscaling/v2): scaleTargetRef points to the Deployment, minReplicas: 2, maxReplicas: 10. Metrics: CPU target utilization 70%, Memory target utilization 80%. Kubernetes scales pod count up/down to maintain the target metric values.

Decision rules:
- Set minReplicas >= 2 for production availability — 1 replica has no fault tolerance
- Use CPU utilization 70% as a target — leaves headroom before pods become saturated
- Combine HPA with PodDisruptionBudget to prevent all replicas from being disrupted simultaneously

Trade-offs:
- HPA reacts to current load — not suitable for sudden traffic spikes; use KEDA for event-driven scaling
- Memory-based scaling can cause scale-thrash if memory is not released promptly after load drops

Anti-patterns:
- Setting minReplicas: 1 in production — a single pod disruption causes a complete outage
- Setting maxReplicas too high without resource quotas — a runaway HPA can exhaust cluster capacity

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Combine HPA with Karpenter on EKS for both pod and node autoscaling
- Use KEDA with SQS queue depth metric for event-driven HPA on EKS

chunks.title: ConfigMap and Secret configuration management
chunks.content:
ConfigMap and Secret configuration management

ConfigMap holds non-sensitive configuration: APP_ENV, LOG_LEVEL, CORS_ORIGINS, MAX_CONNECTIONS. Secrets hold sensitive values (DATABASE_URL) but in production should be managed via External Secrets Operator, not committed as plain Secret manifests. Reference ConfigMap values with valueFrom.configMapKeyRef, Secrets with valueFrom.secretKeyRef.

Decision rules:
- ConfigMap is for non-sensitive configuration only — never put passwords or tokens in ConfigMap
- In production: use External Secrets Operator to sync from AWS Secrets Manager into Kubernetes Secrets
- Reference individual keys (configMapKeyRef, secretKeyRef) rather than envFrom for explicit env var declarations

Trade-offs:
- envFrom (whole ConfigMap/Secret as env vars) is simpler but makes pod environment unpredictable — prefer key-by-key references

Anti-patterns:
- Storing sensitive values in ConfigMap data (not encrypted at rest by default)
- Committing Secret manifests with base64-encoded values to git — base64 is encoding, not encryption

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use External Secrets Operator with AWS Secrets Manager SecretStore for EKS
- Use Secrets Store CSI Driver with AWS SSM Parameter Store as an alternative
